tasks.title: Load against the core count
tasks.statement: The file /proc/loadavg looks like this: "0.61 0.61 0.55 3/828 22084". The first three numbers are the load average for 1, 5, and 15 minutes, the fourth is running tasks / all tasks, the fifth is the last pid. Write a function load_verdict(loadavg, ncpu): ncpu is the core count (nproc prints it). The level comes from the 5-minute load divided by ncpu: below 0.7 is "ok", from 0.7 inclusive to 1.0 is "busy", 1.0 and above is "overloaded". The trend: if the 1-minute load is greater than the 15-minute load times 1.25, it is "rising"; if it is less than the 15-minute load times 0.75, it is "falling"; otherwise "steady". Return a tuple (level, trend).
tasks.hint: Split the line with split() and convert the first three fields to float.

tasks.title: A vmstat verdict
tasks.statement: You get the text of "vmstat 1 N" output: two header lines (the first starts with the word procs, the second with the column names r b swpd free ...; find the columns by that line, because the set may differ, for example there can be a gu column) and lines of plain numbers. The first line of numbers is the average since boot, drop it. Write a function vmstat_verdict(text, ncpu): from the averages of the remaining lines return the first matching verdict in this order: "memory" if the mean of si+so is at least 100; "io" if the mean of wa is at least 20 and the mean of b is at least 1; "steal" if the mean of st is at least 10 (if there is no st column count it as 0); "cpu" if the mean of r is strictly greater than ncpu; otherwise "ok". If no line remains after dropping the first, return "nodata".
tasks.hint: The header is the line whose first token is r; data lines are those where all tokens are numbers. Take each column's index from the header.

tasks.title: Disk saturation from iostat -x
tasks.statement: You get the output of "iostat -x 1 N": several reports, an avg-cpu block before each device table, and a table starts with a line whose first word is Device. The set and order of columns depend on the sysstat version, so find the columns by name in the header: %util, r_await, w_await. The first report is computed from boot, but only the last report matters. Write a function iostat_status(text): return a dictionary device → status for the devices of the last report. Let wait be the larger of r_await and w_await (in milliseconds). If %util is at least 90: "saturated" when wait is at least 20, otherwise "busy" (busy but answering fast, as parallel devices do). If %util is below 90: "slow" when wait is at least 20, otherwise "ok".
tasks.hint: Each time you meet a Device line, remember the new header and reset the collected device rows.

tasks.title: The top header
tasks.statement: You get the header of "top -b -n1" output (procps-ng): the line "%Cpu(s): 3.1 us, 1.0 sy, 0.0 ni, 95.0 id, 0.5 wa, 0.0 hi, 0.2 si, 0.2 st", the lines "MiB Mem : ... total, ... free, ... used, ... buff/cache" and "MiB Swap: ... total, ... free, ... used. ... avail Mem" (older versions use KiB, and some locales use a decimal comma; a number may be glued to the previous comma: "ni,100.0 id"). Write a function top_summary(text) that returns a dictionary: "busy" is 100 minus id, rounded to tenths; "top_state" is the state among us, sy, ni, wa, hi, si, st with the largest value (on a tie, the earlier in that list; "none" if all are zero); "mem_avail_pct" is avail Mem as a percent of the Mem line's total, to tenths; "swap_used_pct" is used as a percent of the Swap line's total, to tenths, 0.0 if there is no swap.
tasks.hint: A regular expression "number, spaces, name" finds all the pairs; replace a decimal comma with a dot. Recognize the Swap line before the Mem line: "avail Mem" sits on it.

tasks.title: Memory from /proc/meminfo
tasks.statement: You get the text of /proc/meminfo (lines "Key:   number kB"). Write a function meminfo_report(text) that returns a dictionary: "used_kb" is MemTotal minus available memory; "naive_used_kb" is the "naive" usage MemTotal − MemFree − Buffers − Cached (not below 0); "avail_pct" is available memory as a percent of MemTotal, to tenths; "swap_used_pct" is used swap as a percent of SwapTotal, to tenths (0.0 if there is no swap); "verdict". Available memory is MemAvailable; if the line is missing (kernels older than 3.14), estimate it as MemFree + Buffers + Cached + SReclaimable. The verdict in order: "critical" if avail_pct is below 5; "low" if below 15; "swap-heavy" if swap_used_pct is at least 50; otherwise "ok".
tasks.hint: Split lines at the first colon and take the first word after it as the number.

tasks.title: PSI pressure
tasks.statement: The files /proc/pressure/cpu, memory and io contain lines like "some avg10=12.40 avg60=8.10 avg300=3.00 total=482011" and, except for the CPU on older kernels, a "full ..." line with the same fields. Write a function psi_levels(files): files is a dictionary "resource → file text". For each resource take avg10 of the some and full lines (a missing line counts as 0; for the cpu resource always ignore the full line: it is undefined system-wide). A resource is "critical" if full is at least 10 or some is at least 40; "warn" if some is at least 10; otherwise leave it out. Return a list of tuples (resource, level): critical first, then warn, inside a level by descending some, on a tie by resource name.
tasks.hint: Split each line into tokens; the fields after the first word are key=value pairs, so dict() them.

tasks.title: Fields of /proc/PID/stat
tasks.statement: A /proc/PID/stat line is "pid (comm) state ppid pgrp ...": 52 space-separated fields, with comm in parentheses, and it may contain spaces and parentheses itself, such as "(Web Content)" or "(a) b (c)". Write a function proc_stat_fields(line, clk_tck, page_size): clk_tck is ticks per second, page_size is the page size in bytes (on arm64 it can be 16384 or 65536). Return a dictionary: "comm" is the name without the outer parentheses; "state" is the state letter (field 3); "ppid" is field 4 (a number); "cpu_seconds" is (utime + stime) / clk_tck, fields 14 and 15, rounded to hundredths; "threads" is num_threads, field 20 (a number); "rss_kb" is rss (field 24, in pages) in kilobytes, an integer.
tasks.hint: The name lies between the first "(" and the last ")" of the line: line.index and line.rindex. The other fields are rest = line[end+1:].split(), and field 3 is rest[0].

tasks.title: CPU between two /proc/stat snapshots
tasks.statement: The "cpu" line in /proc/stat holds cumulative ticks: user nice system idle iowait irq softirq steal guest guest_nice (older kernels have fewer fields: count the missing ones as zeros). Write a function cpu_delta(before, after): before and after are /proc/stat texts at two moments; you need only the summary line "cpu " (not cpu0, cpu1). Take only the first eight counters (guest and guest_nice are already included in user and nice, do not add them), compute the differences and total, their sum. Return a dictionary whose values are percents of total, rounded to tenths: "us" is user + nice, "sy" is system, "id" is idle, "wa" is iowait, "irq" is irq + softirq, "st" is steal, "busy" is everything except idle and iowait. If total is zero, all values are 0.0.
tasks.hint: Find the line whose first word is exactly cpu; take t[1:9] and pad with zeros up to eight.

tasks.title: Retransmits from ss -ti
tasks.statement: The output of "ss -ti" consists of a header line (starting with State) and two-line records: a socket line "ESTAB 0 0 local:port remote:port" and the info line after it, which starts with a space or tab and holds key:value pairs, for example "segs_out:200 ... retrans:2/30 ...". The field retrans:X/Y is printed only when nonzero: X is segments retransmitted and not yet acknowledged, Y is the total retransmits in the life of the connection. Write a function ss_retrans(text, min_ratio): for each connection that has both retrans and segs_out, compute the share Y / segs_out. Return a list of tuples (remote address:port, share rounded to thousandths) for connections with a share of at least min_ratio, by descending share, on a tie by address. The remote address is the fifth word of the socket line (an IPv6 address like [2001:db8::7]:51000 is one word).
tasks.hint: The socket line is the one that does not start with a space or tab. Parse the info tokens with startswith('retrans:') and split('/').

tasks.title: A percentile from a bpftrace histogram
tasks.statement: bpftrace prints a hist() histogram like this: a line "@name:" (or "@name[key]:"), then buckets "[2K, 4K)         40 |@@@@@@@@  |": the bounds, the event count, a bar; other lines and other maps may come before the histogram. Bounds are written as a number with an optional suffix K, M or G (powers of 1024); the closing bracket may be ) or ]; in some versions the first buckets are printed as "[0]" and "[1]", a single value, in which case the lower and upper bounds are equal. Write a function hist_bucket(text, name, pct): name is the exact map name with its key, for example "@lat[sda]" or "@"; pct is an integer percent. Return a tuple (lower, upper) of the bucket bounds as numbers for the bucket where the percentile falls: the needed event count is ceil(total * pct / 100), take the first bucket where the running sum reaches it. If the map is missing or has no events, return None.
tasks.hint: Find the line equal to name + ':' and read the buckets with a regular expression until a blank line or the next map. ceil without math: (total * pct + 99) // 100.
